summary: Mike Krieger, co-founder of Instagram and now a member of technical staff at Anthropic Labs, frames his talk around being unreasonable in what you ask for. He illustrates this with a weekend port of a few hundred thousand lines of Python to TypeScript using Claude Code and a dynamic workflow with Bun, returning Monday to a deployable artifact. He explains that tag-based usage of Claude in Slack is Anthropic's dominant pattern: a multiplayer async paradigm where teammates assign Claude ownership of code areas, monitor feedback channels, and proactively react to API changes. He also recalls two enduring 2010 Instagram scaling lessons: pre-measure everything you might need, and build runtime knobs and feature flags for fast dynamic configuration. On code review, he reframes the bottleneck as comprehension, not time. He describes shipping Claude Code artifacts that travel with a PR to capture intent and trade-offs, and admits he no longer reads every line, instead asking Claude to investigate the questions he would have, calling it Claude-powered but human-driven review. He lays out Labs' organizational model: two-week persevere-or-pivot cycles in which projects are routinely wound down by design, teams assemble fresh around each bet, and bet leads usually manage nobody, keeping the org chart decoupled from projects. Claude Design started ad hoc and solidified only once it shipped and gained traction. Looking forward, he sees Claude Design blurring into apps with persistence, and identifies better inter-surface interoperability as a major unlock, including deleting rigid distinctions between code, co-work, and chat that the average user cannot explain. On startup competition with labs, he draws the Instagram/Google Photos analogy, arguing that startups win through laser focus on a vertical and deep user understanding rather than by outshipping a platform. He closes with sustained emphasis on comprehension, deletion of prescriptive features, and user obsession as the durable advantage. Asked about vertical AI, he highlights finance as a frontier where models improve generation to generation, startups publish useful vertical evals, and the art is finding a cut line that preserves verifiability, audit logging, and data provenance without constraining agentic flexibility; legacy audit systems are often inflexible by design. On mental health, he notes AI cadence is multiples more intense than Instagram-era competition, with a Wednesday all-hands slide tracking the week in AI that often contains a new model, product, or regulatory shift. His advice is to actually take time off, recall that no job is so important you cannot be offline for two days, internalize the "you're never as good as your best game and never as bad as your worst game" cycle, and avoid tying identity to daily launches. He also shares coach-given advice to verbalize emotions openly, which holds space for teammates and lets the group move from shared feeling into problem-solving.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: From CPO to IC at Labs
sections.summary: Introduces Mike Krieger as Instagram co-founder and Anthropic Labs IC. He explains the shift from chief product officer because the FOMO of building with models grew unbearable, a pattern he has seen among former CTOs. He describes the broader paradigm shift from task decomposition to end-state delegation.

sections.title: Be unreasonable in what you ask for
sections.summary: Citing Tariq's earlier keynote phrase, he argues the industry must teach people to be more unreasonable. He critiques first-generation AI products for boxing models in with limited tool access, and contrasts that with newer products like Co-Work that give models a virtual machine and bash access, enabling real remediation work.

sections.title: Weekend port of Python to TypeScript
sections.summary: He describes his most unreasonable ask: porting a few hundred thousand lines of Python to TypeScript over one weekend using a dynamic workflow that verified and churned on its own output. He references Bun as a better deployment story and returns Monday to a completed, deployable port.

sections.title: Scaling lessons from 2010 Instagram
sections.summary: He reflects on early Instagram scaling, including Python 3 type hints, Monkey Type for runtime-to-static type capture, and two pieces of advice that stuck: pre-measure everything you might need, and build first-class knobs, feature flags, and dynamic config for fast runtime changes under load.

sections.title: Tagging Claude in Slack and multiplayer delegation
sections.summary: He explains that tagging Claude in Slack is Anthropic's dominant usage pattern, complementing Claude Code's interactive mode. He describes it as multiplayer async delegation where colleagues assign Claude ownership of a code area, monitor feedback channels, and proactively react to API changes, treating it like a teammate with memory and proactivity.

sections.title: Code review bottleneck is comprehension
sections.summary: He reframes the review bottleneck as human ability to conceptualize large AI-generated changes rather than review time, teasing Claude Code artifacts as the new shared review surface.

sections.title: Claude Code artifacts and human-driven review
sections.summary: He explains that 2,000-line PRs now travel with a Claude Code artifact describing intent and trade-offs, that code is verifiable, and that he no longer reads every line. Instead he asks Claude the questions a reviewer would have, calling it Claude-powered but human-driven review, and is willing to fix forward on cosmetic changes.

sections.title: Persevere-or-pivot and Labs org design
sections.summary: He describes Labs' two-week persevere-or-pivot cadence, the routine winding down of projects by design, and the deliberate decoupling of org chart from projects. Bet leads usually manage nobody; engineering managers focus on individual fit and excitement. Claude Design started ad hoc and solidified only after it shipped, gained traction, and warranted a dedicated team.

sections.title: Future of Claude Design
sections.summary: He sees better interaction between Claude Design and other surfaces like Claude Code as a major unlock, and expects the lines between design and full apps to blur further as users build functional HTML/JS artifacts that call for persistence and sharing.

sections.title: Project unship and what to delete
sections.summary: Referencing his Instagram history of pruning products like Burbn, he cites Anthropic's #project-unship Slack channel. Styles was recently unshipped as prescriptive and superseded by skills. He identifies the confusing code vs. co-work vs. chat distinctions as a candidate for deletion so Claude can act unconstrained, avoiding 2020-era copy-paste workflows.

sections.title: Why start a company when labs ship this fast
sections.summary: Drawing the Instagram vs. Google Photos analogy, he argues platforms are constrained by their own integrations. Startups win through laser focus on a vertical and deep user understanding. A small obsessed team still moves faster than a large org, and code was never the limiting factor, taste and user understanding are.

sections.title: Vertical AI and finance
sections.summary: The reviewer transitions to the day for vertical AI and introduces returning speaker Chris Lovejoy, setting up a finance-focused segment.

sections.title: Vertical AI and finance discussion
sections.summary: He highlights finance as a frontier where models improve generation to generation, vertical finance startups publish useful evals that act as a barometer, and the art is finding a cut line that preserves verifiability, audit logging, and data provenance without constraining agentic flexibility. He notes legacy audit systems are, by design, inflexible for agents on top, so opportunity exists on both sides of the stack.

sections.title: Burnout and intensity of the AI era
sections.summary: Asked how to advise 996 workers on burnout, he notes AI cadence is multiples more intense than Instagram-era competition, with a Wednesday all-hands slide tracking a week that already contains a new model, product, or regulatory shift. He advises actually carving time off, states no job is so important you cannot be offline for a couple of days, references Ben Horowitz's "we're effed it's over" chapter, and urges perspective so identity is not driven by daily launches.

sections.title: Verbalizing emotions as a leader
sections.summary: He shares coach-given advice that if you feel something, others on the team likely feel it too, and recommends verbalizing emotions. He recounts kicking off a Labs meeting by openly saying he was sad and frustrated about a shut-down initiative, which held space for teammates to share their feelings before pivoting to what to do about it. The host closes the session by reinforcing mental-health encouragement.

demonstrations: Had Claude port a few hundred thousand lines of Python to TypeScript over a weekend using a dynamic workflow and Bun for deployment, returning Monday to a deployable port.
Described a colleague tagging Claude in Slack to take ownership of a code area, monitor a feedback channel, and react to API changes.
Described attaching a Claude Code artifact to a ~2,000-line PR to communicate intent and trade-offs, then asking Claude to investigate the questions a reviewer would have.
Described kicking off a Labs meeting by openly saying he was sad and frustrated about a shut-down initiative, which held space for teammates to share feelings and then plan next steps.
limitations: First-generation AI products constrained models' tool and environment access, making unreasonable asks hard until products like Co-Work and Claude Code opened up bash, PDF parsing, and broader degrees of freedom.
Anthropic's own products still suffer from poor inter-surface interoperability and confusing distinctions between code, co-work, and chat.
Some features like Styles were unshipped because they were prescriptive and not AGI-filled, while skills handled the use case better.
Legacy systems built for verifiability and auditability in financial services are, almost by design, inflexible for agentic workloads on top.
quantitativeClaims: A few hundred thousand lines of Python were ported to TypeScript in one weekend.
The port was completed over a single weekend with verification and churn on its own output.
Tag-based Claude usage accounts for how roughly 60% of code is written at Anthropic today (stated by interviewer).
Claude Design shipped a big second release in June after starting in an ad hoc way.
Instagram-style 'four to five percent usage' features illustrate the classic disjoint-subset usage problem like Microsoft Word.
The AI industry moves with new models, products, or regulatory shifts fitting into a single Wednesday all-hands slide, contrasted with Instagram-era once-a-year WWDC anxiety.
